title: Dry summers delayed early autumn records of mushroom-forming fungi by 6-8 days per 100 mm water deficit in nine European countries in 1995-2024, also after recorder-effort adjustment
abstract: Question: does the timing of autumn records of mushroom-forming fungi (Agaricomycetes) follow summer water balance and autumn temperature, and how much of the long-term change in record dates is a change in recorder effort? Data: GBIF occurrence counts (CC0 and CC BY records only) per 5-day bin in July-November 1995-2024 for Norway, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Great Britain, Germany, France, Switzerland and Austria, in two separate record types (field observations, 4.28 million records; preserved specimens, 0.41 million). Lichen and moss records of the same countries and bins are the effort reference. Climate: CRU TS 4.09 country means. Method: dates of the 10%, 50% and 90% record quantiles, raw and as an effort-adjusted index; country fixed effects and country trends; errors clustered by year; two periods (1995-2009, 2010-2024); placebo, leave-one-country-out, latitude-band and 2018 out-of-sample checks. Main result: a wetter June-August made the 10% date earlier by 8.1 +/- 1.1 days per 100 mm in observations and by 7.2 +/- 1.1 in specimens. The sign was negative in both periods, with effort adjustment (-7.8 and -5.6), with fixed latitude bands (-4.5), and in 16 of 17 single-country fits. Next-year water balance had no link, and lichen and moss records did not move with water balance. The 2018 drought delayed the 10% date in 7 of 8 countries for observations, as predicted, but in only 4 of 8 for specimens. Warm August-October moved the 90% date later by about 3 days per C, but the effort reference also moved, so this link is not separable from recording behaviour. Trends: the median observation date became 3.0 days per decade later, but lichen and moss observations became 6.6 days per decade later; after adjustment the median trend was near zero (-0.8 +/- 0.7). The 90% date stayed 2-3 days per decade later after adjustment. In Finland a southward shift of recording changed the median trend from +2.7 to -0.7 days per decade. Limitations: record dates are not fruiting dates; dataset mix changes; the open-licence filter removes most Danish, Dutch and Belgian data; country-mean climate is coarse; species composition was not modelled; the productivity index gave no consistent result.
